title: From simulation to pedagogy: structured AI standardized patients for clinical communication training validated through multi-model and randomized evaluation
abstract: Standardized patients (SPs) are central to clinical communication training but are constrained by cost, scalability, and reliance on trained actors. We present AI standardized patients (AI-SPs), large language model–driven simulators governed by a three-layer information architecture that modulates disclosure according to learner skill. We validate this approach across three phases. In Phase 1, blinded expert evaluation of 350 simulated consultations from five frontier LLMs showed that learner skill level, rather than model choice, drove performance variation (η2 = 0.31 vs 0.06), indicating that pedagogical quality emerges from architec-tural design rather than model scaling. In Phase 1b, 155 live student consultations revealed systematic failures in eliciting safety-critical information, generating automated curriculum diagnostics without expert observation. In a three-arm pilot randomized controlled trial (Phase 2, n = 58), AI-SP training achieved skill gains non-inferior to human SP practice, with a distinctive self-efficacy benefit unique to the AI-SP arm. These findings suggest that architecture-driven AI-SPs offer a scalable, model-portable paradigm for clinical communication training.Competing Interest StatementThe authors have declared no competing interest.Funding StatementThis research received no specific grant from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agency.Author DeclarationsI confirm all relevant ethical guidelines have been followed, and any necessary IRB and/or ethics committee approvals have been obtained.YesThe details of the IRB/oversight body that provided approval or exemption for the research described are given below:The ethics committee of The First Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University waived ethical approval for this work, on the basis that it constitutes an educational research study on medical students with informed written consent and no patient-identifying clinical data.I confirm that all necessary patient/participant consent has been obtained and the appropriate institutional forms have been archived, and that any patient/participant/sample identifiers included were not known to anyone (e.g., hospital staff, patients or participants themselves) outside the research group so cannot be used to identify individuals.YesI understand that all clinical trials and any other prospective interventional studies must be registered with an ICMJE-approved registry, such as ClinicalTrials.gov. output.evidence_of_randomization: In a three-arm pilot randomized controlled trial (Phase 2, n = 58), AI-SP training achieved skill gains non-inferior to human SP practice.
output.reasoning: The manuscript analyzes empirical data from multiple phases of research, including a three-arm pilot randomized controlled trial with 58 participants. However, the outcomes measured are educational/pedagogical in nature (skill gains, self-efficacy) rather than patient-level health or clinical outcomes. The study evaluates the effectiveness of an AI-driven educational tool for training medical students in clinical communication, not the health outcomes of patients receiving clinical care. While the abstract mentions "randomized controlled trial," the randomization appears to apply to the allocation of students to different training modalities (AI-SP vs. human SP), not to patients receiving a health intervention. This is an educational intervention study, not a clinical trial evaluating patient health outcomes, and therefore does not meet CONSORT eligibility criteria.
